facts.claim: High consumption of breakfast cereals is linked to a lower mortality risk.
facts.quote: However, breakfast cereals were associated with a lower mortality risk (RR = 0. 85, 95% CI, 0. 79, 0. 92).

facts.claim: Each 10% increase in ultra-processed food consumption in daily calorie intake is linked to a 15% higher risk of all-cause mortality.
facts.quote: each 10% increase in UPF consumption in daily calorie intake was associated with a 15% higher risk of all-cause mortality (OR = 1. 15; 95% CI: 1. 09, 1. 21; I2 = 0. 0%; p < 0. 001).

facts.claim: In a trial of 20 weight-stable adults, an ultra-processed diet caused an energy intake that was 508 ± 106 kcal/day greater than an unprocessed diet.
facts.quote: Energy intake was greater during the ultra-processed diet (508 ± 106 kcal/day; p = 0. 0001), with increased consumption of carbohydrate (280 ± 54 kcal/day; p < 0. 0001) and fat (230 ± 53 kcal/day; p = 0. 0004), but not protein (-2 ± 12 kcal/day; p = 0. 85).

facts.claim: Highest consumption of ultra-processed foods is linked to an increased risk of all-cause mortality in five studies.
facts.quote: highest UPF consumption was found to be associated with increased risk of all-cause mortality in five studies (risk ratio (RR) 1·25, 95 % CI 1·14, 1·37; P < 0·00001)
facts.causalWarning: causal wording, but the cited study only shows an association

rejected.claim: Participants in a trial gained 0. 9 ± 0. 3 kg during an ultra-processed diet and lost 0. 9 ± 0. 3 kg during an unprocessed diet.
rejected.quote: Weight changes were highly correlated with energy intake (r = 0. 8, p < 0. 0001), with participants gaining 0. 9 ± 0. 3 kg (p = 0. 009) during the ultra-processed diet and losing 0. 9 ± 0. 3 kg (p = 0. 007) during the unprocessed diet.

research.angle: While a controlled trial shows ultra-processed diets cause an increase of about 500 calories a day and weight gain, other studies show that breakfast cereals may actually reduce mortality risk.
research.verdict: The evidence shows that ultra-processed foods cause higher calorie intake and weight gain in a controlled setting and are linked to increased mortality risks in observational studies.
research.caveat: The evidence for mortality risk comes from observational studies, while the evidence for increased calorie intake comes from a small trial of only 20 adults.
